chronic administration of the corticotropin-releasing factor receptor 1 antagonist, antalarin, to Fawn-Hooded rats, a strain with a high propensity to drink alcohol, increases tyrosine hydroxyylase mRNA expression in the ventral mesencaphalon and decreases dopamine transporter binding in the striatum, and increases spine density on medium spiny neurone dendrites.

the neurobiological mechanisms underlying the anxiolytic effects of antalarmin and the reduction in ethanol consumption in Faw‐Hooded Rats.
the effects of stress on the brain and behaviour.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
chronic treatment of Fawn‐hooded rats with antalarmin results in a reduction in the density of striatal dopamine transporter binding sites and an increase in the density of dopamine D2 receptors.
antalarmin treatment increases dopamine release, which may be due to an increased firing rate in dopamine neurons.

antalarmin treatment is associated with a reduction in dopamine transporter binding and an increase in dopamine D2 binding in striatum and that this is associated with an increase in the number of spines on medium spiny neurone dendrites, suggestive of an increase in the efficacy of dopamine neurotransmission in the striatum.
The main takeaway from our work is that
chronic treatment with CRF1R antagonists may ultimately alter postsyaptic signaling mechanisms within reward pathways.
chronic treatment with antalarmin, a selective, centrally acting CRF1 antagonist, regulates the dopamineric system in Fawn-Hooded rats.

chronic antalarmine treatment increases spine density and dopamine D2 receptor density, which is likely to be a consequence of increased dopamine release in the basal ganglia, which is a brain region that is critical for the control of goal‐directed behaviours.
